So, while we want to catch every error, sometimes the best way to handle them is not to trap and not to exit, but to do
something else. So, in C++, we have four different ways of saying how a contract should be handled. The first one is ignore. This check
exists. We've compiled it. We've ran it through the the checker. Everything in it is valid code, but we're choosing not to actually check it.
So, we're not at runtime seeing if it if it succeeds, and it probably succeeds, but we don't look at it. The second option is observe. In this
case, we are checking the contract. We're seeing if it fails, and we are logging that it fails. We're handling a contract violation, but if it returns and it says, "Please
keep going," we're just going to keep going. The third option is enforce. And in enforce, we check it. We let We call the contract violation handler to
see when it fails. Except in this case, we are going to guarantee that there is no possible way you can enter this function. Which means that if your contract
violation handler throws, it's going to throw over your function, it's going to exit. If your contract violation handler doesn't throw, but tries to return,
the compiler is going to make sure it terminates. No matter what, your compiler is going to make sure your function never gets entered if the
contract doesn't hold. And we have quick enforce. And quick enforce is the quick way to do it, but more accurately, it doesn't give you a hook to do
anything. It doesn't call a contract violation handler, it just says, "I'm going to check this, and if it fails, we terminate right here, right now."
We don't have a contract violation. We don't have anything in our binary that says what we're checking, any logging that says what we might be doing, or
what we are failing on. So, for the security case, this is the one you want. And this is most of the time where people look at
these four options and wonder, "Why should I use any of these? Should I be checking any of these? Should I be picking one based on some criteria?"
And there's a really simple answer. You almost always enforce. The thing you want to do is you have something you checked in your code. If
it ever fails, that means your code went off the rails. You want to check that as often as you can. So, the only reasons to use the other
ones are, for the first one, if it's broken or too expensive to run, then we want to ignore it. Especially in the case where you've
written a broken check. You want to be able to turn that off without needing to recompile everything from scratch and deploy 6 hours later.
The second one is if I'm writing something new. For example, if the in the sign function, I'm just adding the pre-contract saying that my angle has to
